title: Margaret Brown: Unsinkable Witness
dek: Titanic survivor who turned sudden fame into relief, suffrage, labor, and humanitarian work.
mortality_event: Survived the 1912 Titanic sinking in Lifeboat 6, then organized survivor relief aboard the Carpathia and used her public platform for reform.
citation_passage: Margaret Tobin Brown (1867–1932), later widely called Molly Brown, was an American philanthropist and activist whose public life extended far beyond the Titanic legend. The State Historical Society of Missouri records that she helped passengers into Lifeboat 6 after the Titanic struck an iceberg in 1912, maintained morale while survivors waited, and helped organize relief for destitute passengers after the Carpathia rescue. Brown used wealth from her family’s Colorado mining interests to support charities, children, and social reform. The Colorado Women’s Hall of Fame notes her work for women’s suffrage, aid to families affected by the Ludlow mining disaster, and preservation in Denver. This obituary comic follows the contradiction between the famous survivor’s nickname and the larger record of organizing, advocacy, travel, and generosity. Brown died in New York City in 1932. The account draws on Britannica, the State Historical Society of Missouri, and the Colorado Women’s Hall of Fame.
page_summaries: Margaret Tobin grows up in Hannibal, Missouri, before work and family obligations bring her to Colorado.
Marriage and the Little Jonny Mine’s wealth give Brown resources that she redirects toward civic life.
Brown becomes active in Denver reform, philanthropy, and organizations working for women and children.
The Titanic disaster places Brown in Lifeboat 6, where she helps passengers and sustains morale.
After rescue by the Carpathia, Brown helps organize relief for survivors who lack resources.
Brown uses public attention for suffrage, humanitarian aid, labor solidarity, and preservation work.
Brown dies in 1932, leaving a legacy larger than the Unsinkable Molly Brown legend.

title: Audre Lorde: Cancer Journals
dek: The poet who made illness, identity, and survival impossible to keep private.
mortality_event: 1977 breast-cancer diagnosis and mastectomy; later liver cancer before her death in 1992, after The Cancer Journals turned illness into public witness.
citation_passage: Audre Lorde (1934–1992) was an American poet, essayist, librarian, and feminist whose work confronted racism, sexism, homophobia, illness, and silence. After a breast-cancer diagnosis and mastectomy in 1977, she recorded the treatment, fear, anger, and isolation surrounding the experience, especially for a Black lesbian woman. Those reflections became The Cancer Journals in 1980, an illness narrative that challenged expectations that women conceal bodily loss or make recovery comfortable for others. This obituary comic follows Lorde from the public voice she built before cancer through diagnosis, surgery, writing, community, and her continuing insistence that difference could be a source of knowledge and power. It closes with her death from cancer in 1992 and the survival of her words. The account is grounded in biographies and records from the National Women’s History Museum, Smithsonian NMAAHC, Poetry Foundation, and her New York Times obituary.
page_summaries: Audre Lorde grows from a young writer into a poet and public speaker who turns survival into language.
Lorde’s poetry confronts racism, sexism, homophobia, and enforced silence before her cancer diagnosis.
A 1977 breast-cancer diagnosis brings Lorde into treatment and makes the body part of her written record.
After mastectomy, Lorde rejects pressure to conceal loss behind a prosthesis and continues writing.
The Cancer Journals transforms private treatment and pain into a public resource for women excluded from conventional illness narratives.
Lorde teaches and speaks about difference as a source of freedom, community, and political knowledge.
After Lorde’s 1992 death from cancer, readers carry forward her insistence that survival must be spoken.

title: Oliver Sacks: Gratitude Near the End
dek: The neurologist who made case histories human, then met terminal cancer with attention and gratitude.
mortality_event: Terminal metastatic ocular/uveal melanoma in 2015, after a 2006 eye tumor, before his final essays collected as Gratitude.
citation_passage: Oliver Sacks (1933–2015) was a neurologist and writer who turned clinical case histories into portraits of individual lives. His 1973 book Awakenings described patients who had survived the encephalitis lethargica epidemic and later received L-Dopa, establishing the humane narrative method that shaped his wider work. Sacks had a retinal melanoma that cost him vision in one eye; when cancer later spread, he announced in 2015 that his remaining time was limited. This obituary comic traces his habits of close attention, his refusal to reduce patients to diagnoses, the reach of Awakenings and later books, and his response to terminal illness. His final essays, collected as Gratitude, considered friendship, work, beauty, mortality, and the value of a singular life. The account draws on the official Oliver Sacks biography and Gratitude pages, plus obituaries from The Guardian and The New York Times.
page_summaries: Oliver Sacks develops the close attention that will shape his work as a neurologist and writer.
In the hospital ward, Sacks treats each patient as a person whose life exceeds any diagnosis.
Awakenings brings Sacks to a wide audience by showing illness as a story about lost and recovered time.
Sacks’s books give neurology a humane voice through accounts of memory, music, perception, and individual lives.
After cancer returns as a terminal illness in 2015, Sacks responds through the discipline of attention.
Sacks writes his final essays about friendship, work, beauty, mortality, and gratitude.
Sacks leaves readers a method: see the person rather than the label and keep the world vivid.

title: Django Reinhardt: Two-Finger Fire
dek: The guitarist whose burned hand helped invent jazz manouche.
mortality_event: A 1928 caravan fire severely burned his left hand; he rebuilt his guitar technique around two working fingers and changed jazz guitar.
citation_passage: Django Reinhardt (1910–1953) was a Belgian-born Romani jazz guitarist and composer whose damaged left hand helped shape a new musical language. In October 1928, a fire swept through his caravan and badly burned him. He lost the use of the third and fourth fingers of his fretting hand, but during convalescence he relearned guitar around the two fingers that still moved freely. The resulting speed, phrasing, and chord technique became central to his unmistakable style. This obituary comic follows his caravan childhood, the fire, the hospital prognosis, the physical work of rebuilding his playing, and his later partnership with violinist Stéphane Grappelli. Together they led the all-string Quintette du Hot Club de France and helped establish the style now called gypsy jazz or jazz manouche. Reinhardt died in 1953 at forty-three. The account is grounded in Britannica, The Guardian’s history of the fire, and Fretboard Journal’s recording history.
page_summaries: Young Django Reinhardt grows up around caravans, dances, and string music, learning to play before settling anywhere.
A 1928 caravan fire badly burns Reinhardt’s left hand and threatens his future as a musician.
During convalescence, Reinhardt faces a damaged fretting hand and a medical prognosis that his guitar playing is finished.
Reinhardt rebuilds his technique around the two fretting fingers that still move freely.
In Paris, Reinhardt and violinist Stéphane Grappelli turn the new technique into the sound of the Quintette du Hot Club de France.
Reinhardt carries his guitar through wartime danger, continuing to compose and perform amid smoke and uncertainty.
After Reinhardt’s death at forty-three, jazz manouche guitarists continue learning from the technique forged after the fire.

title: Terry Fox: Marathon of Hope
dek: The young runner who turned an amputated leg and an unfinished road into a living cancer-research movement.
mortality_event: Diagnosed with osteosarcoma at 18, Terry Fox lost his right leg, ran the 1980 Marathon of Hope across Canada, and stopped near Thunder Bay after cancer spread to his lungs before his death in 1981.
citation_passage: Terry Fox (1958–1981) was a Canadian runner who made cancer research the purpose of his Marathon of Hope. After bone cancer led to the amputation of a leg at eighteen, his experience of other patients' suffering prompted him to plan a run across Canada. He began on April 12, 1980, at the Atlantic Ocean and ran close to a marathon each day. Cancer in his lungs forced him to stop near Thunder Bay, Ontario, on September 1, after 143 days and 5,373 kilometres. Fox died on June 28, 1981, aged twenty-two. The annual Terry Fox Run continued his fundraising effort after his death. This seven-page biographical comic follows the connection between his illness, the unfinished journey, and the cancer-research movement that carried his work forward.

title: Virginia Hall: The Limping Lady
dek: The spy who turned a wooden leg, a radio, and a network into Allied resistance.
mortality_event: After losing her lower left leg in a hunting accident, Virginia Hall used a wooden prosthetic named Cuthbert while serving with SOE and OSS in occupied France, evading the Gestapo and organizing Resistance networks.
citation_passage: Virginia Hall was an American intelligence officer who supported resistance networks in occupied France during World War II. A hunting accident cost her the lower part of her left leg; she used a prosthesis she called Cuthbert. Working first for Britain's Special Operations Executive and later for the American Office of Strategic Services, she organized safe houses, helped prisoners escape, and transmitted intelligence. She later joined the CIA. This seven-page biographical comic follows the dangers of clandestine work and the practical cooperation behind her missions. The CIA's account provides a starting point for checking the historical background.

title: Dith Pran: Killing Fields
dek: The Cambodian photojournalist who survived genocide and turned memory into witness.
mortality_event: Khmer Rouge forced labor, starvation, and escape through Cambodia’s killing fields before later public testimony.

sources.name: The Dith Pran Foundation: About Dith Pran

citation_passage: Dith Pran was a Cambodian photojournalist and interpreter who survived the Khmer Rouge genocide. In 1975 he worked with New York Times reporter Sydney Schanberg during the fall of Phnom Penh. While foreign reporters could leave, Pran remained in Cambodia, concealing his education and enduring forced labor and starvation. He escaped to Thailand in 1979 and later worked as a New York Times photographer in the United States. He also advocated for recognition of genocide victims. This seven-page biographical comic follows survival and the work of bearing witness. The Dith Pran Foundation's account provides context for his life and reporting.

title: Srinivasa Ramanujan: Mock Theta
dek: The dying mathematician whose last formulas kept opening doors.
mortality_event: Final illness and January 1920 letter to Hardy describing mock theta functions before his death at 32.
citation_passage: Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920) was an Indian mathematician whose letters and notebooks contained results that continued to challenge researchers after his death. His correspondence with G. H. Hardy led to a scholarship and, in 1914, a move to Cambridge, where they collaborated on mathematical problems including integer partitions. Serious illness interrupted his years in England. He returned to India in 1919 and died the following year, aged thirty-two. His unpublished notebooks became a continuing source of mathematical investigation. This seven-page biographical comic focuses on his final illness and unfinished work, placing the last formulas within a short life of sustained mathematical invention.

title: Irena Sendler: Jars of Names
dek: The Polish social worker who helped smuggle children from the Warsaw ghetto — and hid their real names in jars.
mortality_event: Gestapo arrest, torture, and death sentence in 1943 before Żegota bribed a guard and she survived underground.
citation_passage: Irena Sendler (1910–2008) was a Polish social worker who helped rescue Jewish children from the Warsaw ghetto during the Holocaust. As head of the children's section of Żegota, the underground Council for Aid to Jews, she worked to move children into hiding and provide new identities. She kept coded records of their original names and placements so surviving relatives could find them after the war. The Gestapo arrested and tortured her in 1943 and sentenced her to death; Żegota rescued her before execution, and she continued working under another identity. This seven-page comic follows rescue, danger, and the preservation of children's identities within a wider network of help.

title: Ernest Shackleton: Endurance After Ice
dek: The Antarctic explorer whose failed crossing became one of history’s clearest studies in leadership: when Endurance sank, he brought every man home alive.
mortality_event: Endurance was trapped, crushed, and sank in Antarctic pack ice; Shackleton led the survival effort through Elephant Island, the James Caird crossing, and rescue of the crew.

sources.name: Royal Museums Greenwich Death and Legacy

citation_passage: Ernest Shackleton (1874–1922) was an Antarctic explorer whose Endurance expedition became a struggle to keep its crew alive. In 1914 he set out to cross Antarctica, but pack ice trapped and crushed the ship. The men eventually reached Elephant Island in small boats. Shackleton and five companions sailed the James Caird to South Georgia; he, Tom Crean, and Frank Worsley then crossed the island to reach help. The remaining men on Elephant Island were rescued in August 1916, and all of the Endurance party survived. Shackleton died during a later expedition in 1922. This seven-page comic follows the decisions and shared effort that turned a failed crossing into a rescue.

title: Paul Kalanithi: Breath Becomes Air
dek: Stanford neurosurgeon and writer whose posthumous memoir turned a terminal diagnosis into a lucid witness on medicine, mortality, fatherhood, and meaning.
mortality_event: Diagnosed with stage IV metastatic lung cancer at 36 near the end of neurosurgery training; died in 2015 while writing When Breath Becomes Air.
citation_passage: Paul Kalanithi (1977–2015) was a neurosurgeon and writer whose lung-cancer diagnosis changed his position from physician to patient near the end of his training. His writing considered how illness alters the experience of time, work, and a future that once seemed predictable. He became a father and completed his Stanford neurosurgery residency while living with the disease. He died aged thirty-seven while working on When Breath Becomes Air, the memoir later named a Pulitzer Prize finalist. This seven-page biographical comic follows medicine, illness, fatherhood, and writing, using his life to explore the questions about meaning that remained when his professional plans changed.

title: Flannery O'Connor: Lupus and Grace
dek: The Southern Gothic writer who made a shortened life speak in hard comic grace.
mortality_event: Diagnosed with lupus in 1950 — the disease that had killed her father — O'Connor spent her final fourteen years writing major fiction from Andalusia farm before dying at 39.
citation_passage: Flannery O'Connor was an American novelist and short-story writer whose fiction combined dark humor, violence, and questions of religious grace. After a serious attack of lupus, she returned to Georgia and lived at Andalusia, her family's farm near Milledgeville. She continued writing, corresponding, and sometimes traveling to give readings while managing illness and treatment. Her books include Wise Blood and A Good Man Is Hard to Find. She died in 1964 at thirty-nine. This eight-page biographical comic considers her writing life alongside physical limits. The New Georgia Encyclopedia's biography offers historical context for reading the story.

title: Mary Anning: Stone and Light
dek: The fossil hunter who survived lightning and taught science to read deep time.
mortality_event: Survived a lightning strike as an infant, then spent a short life uncovering extinct worlds from the Lyme Regis cliffs before dying of breast cancer at 47.
citation_passage: Mary Anning (1799–1847) was a fossil collector and pioneering paleontologist from Lyme Regis on England's Jurassic Coast. She learned to find and prepare fossils with her father and developed her knowledge of geology and anatomy through study. After her brother Joseph found an ichthyosaur skull, she excavated the rest of its skeleton. Her later discoveries included a complete plesiosaur skeleton and a pterosaur. Scientists studied and purchased her finds, but often failed to credit her contribution, and the Geological Society did not admit women. She died of breast cancer aged forty-seven. This eight-page biographical comic follows a short life whose patient work helped reveal extinct forms of life.

title: John Milton: Darkness Visible
dek: The blind poet who dictated Paradise Lost after sight failed.
mortality_event: Became totally blind by about 1652, then dictated Paradise Lost and other late works.

sources.name: Academy of American Poets — John Milton

citation_passage: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and political writer who continued his literary work after losing his sight. His life spanned the English Civil War, the Commonwealth, and the Restoration, and his public writing included arguments about freedom of the press. By the early 1650s he was blind, but he continued working with assistance. Paradise Lost, first published in 1667, tells of Satan, Adam and Eve, and the loss of Eden in blank verse. Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes followed in 1671. This eight-page biographical comic centers on blindness and the sustained work of composition, placing the late poems within a life shaped by political upheaval and personal loss.

title: Jacques Lusseyran: Light in Darkness
dek: Blind French Resistance organizer, Buchenwald survivor, and author of And There Was Light.
mortality_event: Blinded in childhood, then arrested for Resistance work and deported to Buchenwald before surviving to write and teach about inner light.
citation_passage: Jacques Lusseyran (1924–1971) was a French Resistance organiser, concentration-camp survivor, teacher, and writer. He lost his sight in a childhood accident and continued his education in Paris. The Buchenwald Memorial describes his role in a student resistance group that joined Défense de la France in 1943, when he helped distribute its underground newspaper. The Gestapo arrested him that year. In January 1944 he was deported to Buchenwald, where he used his knowledge of languages to interpret information in the Little Camp. Following liberation in April 1945, he studied literature and philosophy at the Sorbonne, later teaching in France and the United States. His autobiographical writing addressed blindness and imprisonment. Final Notes' seven-page comic, Light in Darkness, follows his resistance work and survival. The linked memorial biography supplies historical context; the comic's imagery is a creative interpretation rather than a primary historical record.
page_summaries: Jacques Lusseyran runs through Paris before a childhood accident leaves his eyes bandaged. Panels of hands touching a cup, a window and a book use golden lines to introduce the comic’s inner-light motif.
Under the occupation of France, Lusseyran listens as students gather around papers. The sequence moves from marching figures in the street to quiet meetings and his hands finding a wall at night.
Lusseyran and fellow Resistance members meet by candlelight, print leaflets and pass papers between doorways. Close-ups of listening faces connect their underground work with trust and attention.
A meeting gives way to a police raid, questioning and a crowded deportation train. A golden line follows Lusseyran’s hand against the train’s wooden interior.
At Buchenwald, prisoners stand outside barracks, whisper to one another and offer a supporting hand. The final group gathers around a small light, continuing the comic’s image of solidarity.
The sequence turns from camp memories to manuscripts, a classroom and Lusseyran speaking to students. An illuminated book connects his writing and teaching with the experiences he survived.
A road scene and an empty chair mark Lusseyran’s death in 1971. Candles, pages and a group of readers revisit his life, ending with attention as the comic’s lasting theme.

title: Maya Angelou: Caged Bird Voice
dek: The poet who turned years of silence into a public language of survival.
mortality_event: Childhood trauma and years of mutism before literature, mentorship, memoir, and civil-rights witness returned her voice to the world.
citation_passage: Maya Angelou (1928–2014) was an American writer, performer, and civil-rights activist whose autobiographical work brought personal experience into public literature. Childhood sexual violence was followed by years in which she did not speak; reading and poetry remained part of her life. Her memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings recounts her early years, including trauma and racism. Angelou also worked as a singer and dancer, served the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, wrote poetry and essays, and taught at Wake Forest University. This seven-page biographical comic follows the relationship between silence, language, and the wider creative and public work through which she became known.

title: Wilma Rudolph: The Girl Who Outran the Brace
dek: A child marked by polio became the first American woman to win three track-and-field gold medals at one Olympics.
mortality_event: Childhood polio and illness impaired her left leg before she learned to walk, run, and win three gold medals at Rome 1960.

sources.name: National Women's History Museum: Wilma Rudolph

citation_passage: Wilma Rudolph was an American sprinter who became the first American woman to win three track-and-field gold medals at a single Olympic Games, in Rome in 1960. Childhood polio had required her to wear a leg brace, with her family helping care for her. She first excelled at basketball before turning to track. After her Olympic success, she insisted that her hometown celebration be integrated and later worked in education and community sports. This seven-page biographical comic connects childhood illness, athletic training, and public influence. The National Women's History Museum biography offers a source for checking the historical background.

title: The Man Who Moved After Stillness
dek: American actor and disability advocate who turned life after a 1995 spinal-cord injury into a public fight for paralysis research, access, and dignity.
mortality_event: 1995 equestrian accident causing paralysis from the neck down; afterward he used celebrity to build spinal-cord research and quality-of-life advocacy before his death in 2004.
citation_passage: Christopher Reeve (1952–2004) was an American actor, director, and advocate for people living with paralysis. Known internationally for playing Superman, he sustained a spinal-cord injury in a riding competition on May 27, 1995. After rehabilitation, he used his public profile to press for research funding and better quality of life for the paralysis community. His creative work continued: he directed In the Gloaming and published the autobiography Still Me. This six-page biographical comic follows the injury and the work that came afterward, including advocacy, research support, and efforts to make disabled people's needs heard in public life.

title: The Tormented Light
dek: Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who created over 2,000 artworks in a decade, most in the final years before his death at 37.
mortality_event: 1888 ear mutilation and asylum commitment — between psychotic episodes, he painted The Starry Night, Irises, and 150 other masterpieces before his death in 1890.

sources.name: Van Gogh Museum — Illness and the Healing Power of Art

citation_passage: Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) was a Dutch artist whose paintings, drawings, and letters record sustained work amid periods of serious illness. After a crisis in Arles in December 1888, he experienced further attacks and hospital stays. In May 1889 he voluntarily entered Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy, where he used a room as a studio and painted when well enough. His brother Theo remained an important source of support. The exact nature of his illness remains uncertain. This eight-page biographical comic focuses on the relationship between illness and artistic work, with the museum's account and his letters providing context for a life often reduced to its most dramatic incidents.

title: Helen Keller: The Hand That Found Water
dek: A fever closed sight and sound; touch reopened the world.
mortality_event: At nineteen months, an acute illness left Helen Keller deafblind; at the water pump in 1887, language broke through by touch.
citation_passage: Helen Keller (1880–1968) was an American deafblind author and activist whose education began with sustained support from Anne Sullivan. At a water pump in 1887, Sullivan spelled the word for water into Keller's hand while water flowed over the other, helping her connect a word with what it named. That episode was part of a much longer education. Keller graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904 and published The Story of My Life while still a student. Her writing and public advocacy continued for decades. This seven-page biographical comic follows illness, tactile language, and learning, with the later author and advocate providing context beyond the famous childhood scene.

title: Roald Dahl: Crash and Chocolate
dek: The pilot who survived the desert and gave children dangerous stories.
mortality_event: 1940 RAF crash in the Libyan desert causing skull fracture, facial injuries, and temporary blindness.

sources.name: RAF Benevolent Fund: Roald Dahl’s RAF career

citation_passage: Roald Dahl was a British writer whose career included wartime service as a Royal Air Force pilot. In September 1940, unable to find his destination airstrip, he crash-landed in the North African desert and escaped his burning aircraft. After hospital treatment and rehabilitation, he returned to flying. His account of the ordeal later reached the Saturday Evening Post, and he went on to write children's stories including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. This seven-page biographical comic considers danger, recovery, and storytelling. The RAF Benevolent Fund describes his military career; the official biography also acknowledges the harm of his antisemitic remarks.

title: George Orwell: The Throat of Truth
dek: The writer who survived a bullet through the throat and gave power a name.
mortality_event: Shot through the throat by a sniper in the Spanish Civil War in 1937; survived to write Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four before dying of tuberculosis in 1950.
citation_passage: George Orwell (1903–1950), the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. In 1937 he fought as a Republican volunteer in the Spanish Civil War and survived a bullet wound to the throat. His account of Spain, Homage to Catalonia, appeared in 1938. Animal Farm followed in 1945, and Nineteen Eighty-Four in 1949. He completed the latter while his health worsened, and died of tuberculosis in January 1950. This seven-page biographical comic follows the throat injury and the later writing, connecting his experience of political violence with his continuing attention to power and language.

title: The Merchant of Death
dek: Swedish inventor and industrialist whose 1895 will established the foundation for the Nobel Prizes.
mortality_event: The comic pairs family loss with a commonly retold premature-obituary story to explore mortality and legacy; the documented 1895 will funds the Nobel Prizes.

sources.name: Norwegian Nobel Institute — Alfred Nobel's will

citation_passage: Alfred Nobel (1833–1896) was a Swedish inventor and industrialist whose fortune became the basis of the Nobel Prizes. His final will, signed in Paris on November 27, 1895, directed income from a fund toward prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace. He asked that recipients be chosen without regard to nationality. The first prizes were awarded in 1901, after disputes over the will were resolved. This eight-page comic considers mortality and legacy through a premature-obituary story. That story's influence on his decision is not established here; the will itself documents the lasting institutions he intended to fund.
story_notes: The comic uses a premature-obituary account to explore Nobel's legacy. The sources checked for this introduction establish the contents of his will, but do not establish that an obituary caused his decision.

Nobel's final will specifies five prize fields and asks that recipients be chosen without regard to nationality. The Norwegian Nobel Institute documents the will, the disputes over it, and the first awards in 1901.

title: Blink Manuscript
dek: French Elle editor who dictated a landmark memoir one eyelid blink at a time.
mortality_event: 1995 stroke causing locked-in syndrome before he dictated The Diving Bell and the Butterfly by blinking.

sources.name: Penguin Random House: The Diving Bell and the Butterfly

citation_passage: Jean-Dominique Bauby was a French journalist and editor of Elle who wrote The Diving Bell and the Butterfly after a brainstem stroke in 1995. Living with locked-in syndrome, he communicated by blinking his left eyelid to select letters as someone recited the alphabet. That collaborative method allowed him to dictate a memoir about hospital life, family, memory, and imagination. He died in 1997, two days after the book's French publication. This seven-page biographical comic follows the practical effort of making a manuscript under severe physical limits. The publisher's account provides background on Bauby and the memoir.

title: The Night That Kept Speaking
dek: Romanian-born Jewish writer, Holocaust survivor, professor, and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whose Night made survivor testimony impossible to ignore.
mortality_event: Survived deportation as a teenager to Auschwitz and Buchenwald before writing Night and becoming a public witness against genocide.
citation_passage: Elie Wiesel (1928–2016) was a Jewish writer, teacher, and Holocaust survivor whose testimony became part of public remembrance. Deported with his family to Auschwitz in 1944, he was selected for forced labor at Monowitz and later transported to Buchenwald, where his father died. After the war he worked as a journalist and author; Night recounts his experiences as a teenager during the Holocaust. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986 and helped bring the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum into being. This seven-page comic follows imprisonment, survival, and the later work of testimony, teaching, and advocacy against oppression.

title: The Captive Who Wrote the Knight
dek: Spanish soldier, captive, playwright, and novelist whose Don Quixote helped invent the modern novel.
mortality_event: Wounded at Lepanto in 1571 and held captive in Algiers for five years before Don Quixote.
citation_passage: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547–1616) was a Spanish soldier and writer best known for Don Quixote. He was seriously wounded at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571. On a later voyage back to Spain, corsairs captured him and his brother and took them to Algiers. Miguel remained captive for five years, attempted escape, and was finally ransomed in 1580. Back in Spain he wrote plays and fiction while also working to support himself. The first part of Don Quixote appeared in 1605. This eight-page biographical comic follows war injury and captivity into the long, uncertain working life that preceded literary success.

title: The Man Who Wrote the Camps
dek: Russian novelist and historian who exposed the Soviet Gulag.
mortality_event: 1945 arrest, eight years in Soviet labour camps, internal exile, and cancer before the works that exposed the Gulag.
citation_passage: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (1918–2008) was a Russian writer whose experience of Soviet imprisonment became material for fiction and historical testimony. Arrested in 1945 for criticizing Stalin in private letters, he was sentenced to eight years in labor camps followed by internal exile. One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, published in 1962, brought camp life into Soviet literature. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970. Publication of The Gulag Archipelago in the West was followed by his forced expulsion from the Soviet Union in 1974; he returned to Russia in 1994. This eight-page comic follows imprisonment, survival, and the writing that made the camps a subject of public witness.

title: The Chemist Who Witnessed
dek: Italian Jewish chemist, Auschwitz survivor, and writer who turned survival into literature
mortality_event: Survived Auschwitz III-Monowitz (1944–45) before writing If This Is a Man and The Periodic Table

sources.name: Centro Internazionale di Studi Primo Levi: Biography

closing_line: The reprieve was one moment. The work was the rest of his life.
citation_passage: Primo Levi was an Italian Jewish chemist, writer, and Holocaust survivor from Turin. Arrested after joining a partisan group, he was deported to Auschwitz in 1944 and imprisoned at Monowitz. His chemical training led to work in a camp laboratory; help from the Italian civilian Lorenzo Perrone also mattered to his survival. After returning to Italy, he wrote If This Is a Man while rebuilding his working and family life. This eight-page biographical comic considers survival, testimony, and the responsibility of describing what happened. The Primo Levi study center's chronology connects his experience with his later writing.

title: Henri Matisse: The Second Life
dek: French modernist painter who turned illness into a final language of color and scissors.
mortality_event: Near-fatal 1941 surgery for duodenal cancer in Lyon, with complications and long confinement afterward.

sources.name: MoMA — The Cut-Outs: technique and development
Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon — Henri Matisse, le laboratoire intérieur

closing_line: The reprieve was one moment. The work was the rest of his life.
citation_passage: Henri Matisse (1869–1954) was a French artist whose late cut-outs combined painted paper, scissors, and arrangements of vivid shapes. In 1941 he underwent surgery for duodenal cancer in Lyon. His subsequent work continued a long exploration of color and line: he had used cut paper for designs well before the operation, and the technique developed into an independent medium during his final years. Studio assistants painted sheets with gouache; Matisse cut the forms and directed their placement, including large compositions on his studio walls. Works from this period include Jazz (1947) and designs for the Chapel of the Rosary in Vence. This eight-page biographical comic follows his serious illness and the artistic work of his final years.

title: Harriet Tubman: The Road Back
dek: Underground Railroad conductor, abolitionist, Union scout, and suffragist.
mortality_event: Survived a severe head injury from an iron weight while enslaved, then escaped and repeatedly returned to rescue others.
sources: National Park Service — Harriet Tubman National Historical Park

sources.name: National Park Service — Harriet Tubman life and work

closing_line: The reprieve was one moment. The work was the rest of her life.
citation_passage: Harriet Tubman (c. 1822–1913) was an American abolitionist who escaped slavery and repeatedly returned to help others reach freedom. While enslaved in Maryland, she survived a severe head injury after an overseer threw an iron weight. She escaped to Philadelphia in 1849, then made about thirteen return journeys and guided approximately seventy relatives and friends out of slavery. Her knowledge of terrain and underground networks also supported her work for the Union during the Civil War. Afterward she lived in Auburn, New York, and worked for equality and women's voting rights. This eight-page comic follows injury, escape, and the repeated choice to return for others.

title: Time Under Shadow
dek: Theoretical physicist and public explainer who kept thinking about black holes, time, and the universe after a terminal diagnosis tried to close the future.
mortality_event: Diagnosed with motor neurone disease around his 21st birthday and given roughly two years to live before decades of later work on singularities, black holes, and public science.

sources.name: Gonville & Caius: Hawking on the support for his working life

closing_line: The reprieve was one moment. The work was the rest of his life.
citation_passage: Stephen Hawking was a British theoretical physicist and cosmologist who studied black holes and the origins of the universe at Cambridge. His work showed that black holes produce radiation, now known as Hawking radiation. A Brief History of Time, published in 1988, brought cosmology to a broad readership. He lived with motor neurone disease for decades, using a wheelchair and a computerized voice as his disability progressed. This seven-page biographical comic considers scientific work alongside uncertain time and the support needed to continue it. Cambridge's faculty tribute and Hawking's own speech at Caius provide context for his research and working life.

title: After the Raft
dek: Olympic runner, World War II airman, survivor, and public witness to endurance after the Pacific nearly erased him.
mortality_event: Survived a 1943 Pacific crash, 47 days adrift, and nearly two years as a Japanese prisoner of war before his later public testimony and forgiveness work.

closing_line: The reprieve was one moment. The work was the rest of his life.
citation_passage: Louis Zamperini (1917–2014) was an American Olympic runner and wartime airman whose survival extended from a Pacific crash to imprisonment. He competed in the 1936 Berlin Olympics before joining the Army Air Corps. When his B-24 crashed in 1943, he survived 47 days at sea before Japanese forces captured him. He endured prisoner-of-war camps and returned home after the war. His later account described a religious conversion and efforts to forgive former captors. This eight-page biographical comic follows the crash, raft, captivity, and life afterward, treating survival as a continuing story rather than an ending at rescue.

title: The Broken Mirror
dek: Mexican painter whose self-portraits made pain, identity, the body, and death modern art's evidence.
mortality_event: 1925 bus-trolley crash in Mexico City that shattered her body and led to a long recovery in which she began painting.

sources.name: National Museum of Women in the Arts

citable_summary: Frida Kahlo (1907–1954) was a Mexican painter whose self-portraits made pain, disability, identity, and death central evidence in modern art.
At age 18, Kahlo was badly injured in a bus-trolley crash in Mexico City; her long recovery helped turn painting from an interest into a life-defining practice.
This obituary comic frames the crash, the recovery bed, and the mirror as the conditions under which Kahlo began making the images that outlived her.
story_notes: Frida Kahlo did not originally set out to build a public mythology from pain. She was a young pre-medical student before the 1925 bus-trolley crash left her with spinal, pelvic, shoulder, and foot injuries that shaped the rest of her life.

The comic uses the mirror as a practical and symbolic object: while confined during recovery, Kahlo turned her own body and face into available subjects. That constraint became one of the sources of her visual language.

The sources for this page combine a general reference biography, a museum artist profile, an art-history biography, and an editorial account of how Kahlo used clothing, posture, and self-presentation around disability.
page_summaries: Opening page introducing Frida Kahlo and the broken-mirror frame of the comic.
Kahlo's early life and the turn from medical ambition toward a body marked by injury.
The 1925 collision becomes the central mortality event of the story.
Recovery narrows the room but gives the mirror and canvas new force.
Self-portraiture becomes a way to record pain, identity, and survival without softening them.
Kahlo's work grows from private injury into a public visual language.
The body remains damaged, but the paintings keep arguing with disappearance.
Closing page on what survived Kahlo: images that made pain impossible to ignore.
closing_line: The crash broke the plan. The mirror helped build the work that remains.
citation_passage: Frida Kahlo (1907–1954) was a Mexican painter known for self-portraits. Before becoming an artist, she entered a pre-medical programme at fifteen. A severe bus accident three years later left her with multiple injuries and a long recovery. The National Museum of Women in the Arts describes how she began painting in oils during that recovery, drawing on the colours and forms of Mexican folk art. Her subjects included her own face and body, giving experiences of pain and identity a visible form. Kahlo married the muralist Diego Rivera in 1929 and held her first solo exhibition in New York in 1938. Final Notes' eight-page comic, The Broken Mirror, concentrates on the accident, recovery, and turn toward painting. Its mirror is both a subject within that story and a way of framing self-portraiture. The linked sources provide biographical context for this creative interpretation.

title: Meaning Under Ash
dek: Austrian neurologist, psychiatrist, Holocaust survivor, and founder of logotherapy.
mortality_event: Survived Nazi concentration camps including Theresienstadt, Auschwitz, Kaufering, and Türkheim.
citable_summary: Viktor Emil Frankl (1905–1997) was an Austrian neurologist, psychiatrist, Holocaust survivor, and founder of logotherapy, which he named before his imprisonment.
Frankl was deported through Theresienstadt and Auschwitz, then sent to Kaufering and Türkheim, where he reconstructed ideas for his work while ill and imprisoned.
This obituary comic focuses on the loss of family and manuscript, then on Frankl's postwar reconstruction of meaning as clinical theory and testimony.
story_notes: Frankl's story is not simply a survival anecdote. Before deportation, he was already a psychiatrist concerned with suicide, depression, and the human need for meaning.
The comic follows the pressure placed on that work by the camps: family members were murdered, his manuscript was lost, and the question of meaning had to survive contact with catastrophe.

After liberation, Frankl returned to Vienna and wrote the work published in English as Man's Search for Meaning. The page's sources connect his institutional biography, reference biography, and the publication history of the book.
page_summaries: Opening page introducing Viktor Frankl and the search for meaning under catastrophe.
Frankl's early medical and psychiatric work before deportation.
The Nazi camps strip away family, home, and manuscript.
Auschwitz and transfer to forced labor camps become the story's central mortality pressure.
Illness and deprivation test whether meaning can remain more than an idea.
Frankl reconstructs thought under conditions designed to erase personhood.
Liberation leaves grief and the task of rebuilding the work.
Closing page on logotherapy and the book that carried the testimony forward.
closing_line: The camps took his family and a manuscript. The work he rebuilt is what remains.
citation_passage: Viktor Emil Frankl (1905–1997) was an Austrian neurologist and psychiatrist whose work centered on meaning. The Viktor Frankl Institute dates his use of the term logotherapy to 1926, before his imprisonment in Nazi camps. In 1942, he and his family were deported to Theresienstadt. In 1944, he was sent to Auschwitz, then to Kaufering and Türkheim, camps associated with Dachau. His unpublished manuscript was lost at Auschwitz. While ill with typhus at Türkheim, he worked to reconstruct it on scraps of paper. After liberation in 1945, he returned to Vienna, where he learned of further family losses and resumed writing. His camp testimony appeared in German in 1946 and later in English as Man's Search for Meaning. Final Notes' eight-page comic, Meaning Under Ash, follows this relationship between an existing body of thought, catastrophic loss, and the work of rebuilding.

title: Borrowed Time
dek: Russian novelist. Survivor of a staged execution.
mortality_event: 1849 staged execution / mock firing squad at Semyonovsky Square

sources.name: Project Gutenberg — The House of the Dead: text and historical introduction

citable_summary: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoyevsky (1821–1881) was a Russian novelist whose 1849 mock execution and Siberian imprisonment became decisive facts in his later fiction.
Dostoyevsky was arrested over the Petrashevsky Circle, sentenced to death, taken to a firing-squad ritual, and reprieved only at the last moment before being sent to Siberia.
This obituary comic treats the reprieve as borrowed time: the later novels return again and again to freedom, guilt, punishment, faith, and life under extreme moral pressure.
story_notes: Dostoyevsky's near-execution was staged as punishment before exile, but he experienced it as an immediate confrontation with death. That moment became a recurring imaginative source in his mature work.
The comic follows the path from early literary promise to arrest, the square, the lowered guns, prison at Omsk, and the later novels that turned punishment into artistic material.

The source trail combines a reference account of the arrest, an essay on Dostoyevsky's letters and post-prison work, a public-domain text from his prison literature, and a Literary Hub essay on the mock execution's afterlife in the novels.
page_summaries: Opening page introducing Dostoyevsky and the idea of borrowed time.
Early life near suffering and institutions of poverty.
The young writer resists the uniform path expected of him.

The soul goes on trial in the later novels.
St. Petersburg and 1881 frame the end of the life.
Closing page on the work that remains after borrowed time.
closing_line: The reprieve was one moment. The work was the rest of his life.
citation_passage: Fyodor Dostoyevsky (1821–1881) was a Russian novelist whose writing returned to punishment, freedom, and the value of a human life. Sentenced to death in 1849, he received a reprieve and was sent to imprisonment in Siberia. The House of the Dead drew on that experience, portraying prison life through a fictional narrator rather than presenting a simple personal diary. This fourteen-page biographical comic follows the arrest, threatened execution, reprieve, and imprisonment, then turns to the literary work that followed. Its title, Borrowed Time, frames survival as a continuing question about how to live and what to make after an encounter with death.
